# Introduction

## Purpose of the assignment

This study note reproduces the UCLA OARC seminar analyses of the SPSS Anxiety Questionnaire (SAQ-8) using R and lavaan. It connects model syntax, identification, estimated parameters, and fit so that I can use it as a reference when evaluating a measurement model. The current Canvas M11 assignment determines the requirements: an HTML study note and its Quarto source, visible executable code, interpretations, practice answers, and project links.

## CFA and EFA

Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) investigates a scale's possible factor structure when the number of factors or allocation of items is uncertain. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) evaluates a specified measurement structure: which items load on which factors, which cross-loadings are zero, and whether factors correlate. CFA can reject a proposed structure; good fit alone does not prove that a model is uniquely correct or substantively valid. Repeatedly changing a CFA using the same data becomes exploratory and requires independent validation.

## Source review and corrections

I used the UCLA seminar webpage, its video transcript, complete analysis code, and supplementary exercise code. The video is Johnny Lin's May 17, 2021 workshop, published June 4, 2021. Its sequence moves from measurement concepts and identification to standardization, model fit, two-factor CFA, and three exercises. The webpage additionally covers second-order CFA. All numerical output below is generated by the executable chunks, rather than transcribed as if it were newly calculated.

Canvas requires haven, whereas the older UCLA code imports with foreign. I use haven::read_sav() and retain numeric item scores. Several source statements need clarification: the displayed three-item models fix residual covariances to zero, not freely estimate them; standardized=TRUE requests output and does not change identification; std.lv=TRUE changes the factor scale during estimation. A nonsignificant chi-square means failure to reject exact fit, not a significant result. Nonnegative degrees of freedom are necessary but not sufficient for identification. A larger chi-square indicates greater overall weighted discrepancy at a fixed sample size, not that every residual covariance is larger or positive. The wording of Item 6 changes within the seminar, so substantive labels are treated as teaching illustrations, not a validated questionnaire codebook.

# Data and software

## Required packages and reproducibility

Install haven and lavaan once in the R console with install.packages(c("haven", "lavaan"), dependencies=TRUE). Quarto, RStudio or Positron, Git, and a GitHub account support the reproducible workflow. knitr supplies tables during rendering. The appendix records the software session.

```{r}
library(haven)
library(lavaan)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(digits = 3)
# Helpers retain useful numerical precision while making tables readable.
tab <- function(x, caption = NULL) { if (is.matrix(x) && ncol(x)>9) x <- t(x); if (is.data.frame(x)) { if ("op" %in% names(x)) x$op <- paste0(intToUtf8(96),x$op,intToUtf8(96)); if ("pvalue" %in% names(x)) x$pvalue <- format.pval(x$pvalue,digits=3,eps=.001) }; rn <- if (is.data.frame(x) && any(c("Item","Model") %in% names(x))) FALSE else NA; knitr::kable(x, digits=3, caption=caption, row.names=rn) }
parameters <- function(fit) {
p <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE)
p[p$op %in% c("=~", "~~"),
c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est", "se", "pvalue", "std.lv", "std.all")]
}
fitrow <- function(fit) {
fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea",
"rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "rmsea.pvalue",
"srmr", "aic", "bic"))
}
```

## Importing and examining SAQ-8

The source SPSS file has 2,571 cases and 23 items. SAQ-8 refers to its first eight items, not to a file containing only eight columns. The local copy avoids a fresh network download on every render. Numeric conversion removes haven labels from the analysis columns without converting response codes to factors. Missingness and response frequencies are checked before fitting.

```{r}
data_url <- "https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/SAQ.sav"
if (!file.exists("SAQ.sav")) {
download.file(data_url, "SAQ.sav", mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
}
raw <- read_sav("SAQ.sav")
items <- sprintf("q%02d", 1:8)
dat <- as.data.frame(lapply(raw[items], as.numeric))
dim(raw)
str(dat)
head(dat)
tab(data.frame(Item = items, Missing = colSums(is.na(dat)),
Minimum = sapply(dat, min), Maximum = sapply(dat, max)))
lapply(dat, table)
tab(round(cor(dat), 3), "SAQ-8 correlation matrix")
tab(round(cov(dat[c("q03", "q04", "q05")]), 3),
"Sample covariances for the three-item example")
stopifnot(nrow(dat) == 2571, !anyNA(dat))
```

The matrix shows shared variation among many items, but not a uniformly strong single dimension. Items 6 and 7 correlate about .51. Item 2 has weak relationships with most items, while Item 3 has negative associations with most anxiety-oriented items. A correlation matrix has ones on its diagonal and is symmetric; a covariance matrix has item variances on the diagonal. Negative signs require checking item wording and coding. I retain the original scores to reproduce the seminar; reversing an item merely changes its direction and does not automatically repair a poorly fitting measurement structure.

The seminar uses conventional maximum likelihood (ML), treating the five-category scores as approximately continuous. This is a reproduction choice, not a general claim that Likert responses are normally distributed. For a substantive study I would inspect distributions and consider robust ML or an ordinal estimator. Modern lavaan supports ordered indicators, for example ordered=items with WLSMV; the video's statement suggesting categorical CFA is unavailable should not be treated as current software guidance.

# CFA concepts

## Measurement model and model-implied covariances

For item j, the measurement model is

$$y_j = \tau_j + \lambda_j\eta + \epsilon_j.$$

The observed indicator is the questionnaire response; the latent factor is the unobserved construct. The loading is the expected change in the item for a unit change in the factor. Residual variance represents item variation not accounted for by the modeled factor, including item-specific variation and measurement error. It is not necessarily pure random error.

For a first-order CFA,

$$\Sigma(\theta)=\Lambda\Psi\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\Theta.$$

Lambda contains loadings, Psi contains latent variances and covariances, and Theta contains item residual variances and covariances. The model is estimated to reproduce the sample covariance matrix S. The residual covariance matrix is S minus the fitted model-implied covariance matrix. This matrix of discrepancies is different from Theta, the residual covariance parameters within the model. With uncorrelated item errors, a one-factor model implies Cov(y_i,y_j)=lambda_i lambda_j Var(eta) for different items.

## Reading a path diagram

Circles denote latent variables, rectangles denote observed indicators, and triangles denote intercepts. A one-headed arrow from a factor to an item represents a loading; a two-headed arrow between variables represents a covariance, and a curved arrow back to a variable represents its variance. In a three-item example the factor points to q03, q04, and q05, each of which also has an item residual. These arrows describe the proposed measurement structure and do not by themselves establish a causal mechanism.

## Identification and degrees of freedom

For p observed variables, the covariance matrix supplies p(p+1)/2 unique moments. Its upper and lower triangles duplicate one another. Degrees of freedom equal the number of unique observed moments minus the number of independently free parameters, after accounting for constraints.

| Model | Known covariance moments | Independently free parameters | df |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Three indicators, all residual covariances free, no scale constraint | 6 | 10 | -4 |
| Three indicators, zero residual covariances, no scale constraint | 6 | 7 | -1 |
| Three indicators, marker loading fixed | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| Three indicators, factor variance fixed | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| Eight indicators, one factor | 36 | 16 | 20 |
| Seven indicators, orthogonal two factors with equal two-item loadings | 28 | 13 | 15 |
| Seven indicators, correlated two factors | 28 | 15 | 13 |

A fixed parameter has a prespecified value, such as a loading of 1 or a covariance of 0. A free parameter is estimated. An equality constraint links parameters, reducing the number of independent quantities. Under-identification means that the model does not uniquely determine the parameters; negative df immediately signals insufficient moments. A just-identified model has df=0 and imposes no testable covariance restrictions. An over-identified model has positive df and testable restrictions, provided it is identified. Counting alone does not establish a unique solution: scale, nonzero relations, rank, convergence, and admissibility also matter.

Fixing a marker loading sets the factor's units; it does not mean that the item is measured without error. Under marker scaling, two free loadings, three residual variances, and one factor variance total six parameters. Under variance standardization, three loadings plus three residual variances again total six. Freely estimating three item means adds three moments and three intercepts, leaving df unchanged.

# One-factor CFA

## Three-item model: marker versus variance standardization

The expression f =~ q03 + q04 + q05 declares a latent factor f measured by the three named items. The =~ operator specifies measurement, `~~` specifies a variance or covariance, NA* frees a default fixed loading, and 1* fixes a parameter to one. Both approaches below estimate the same covariance structure in different units.

```{r}
# Marker method: q03 loading fixed to 1; factor variance estimated.
m1a <- 'f =~ q03 + q04 + q05'
fit3_marker <- cfa(m1a, data = dat)
summary(fit3_marker, standardized = TRUE)

# Variance method: free q03 loading and fix factor variance to 1.
m1b <- '
f =~ NA*q03 + q04 + q05
f ~~ 1*f
'
fit3_variance <- cfa(m1b, data = dat)
fit3_shortcut <- cfa(m1a, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit3_variance, standardized = TRUE)
standardizedSolution(fit3_marker)
tab(parameters(fit3_marker), "Three-item marker solution")
```

The marker loadings are approximately 1.000, -1.139, and -.945; the factor variance is .340. Under variance scaling the loadings are .583, -.665, and -.551. Std.lv standardizes the latent variable; Std.all standardizes both latent and observed variables. The fully standardized loadings are .543, -.701, and -.572. Thus a one-SD increase in the factor, oriented toward q03, is associated with a .701-SD decrease in q04. Changing the factor's orientation would reverse all loadings without changing fit.

The unstandardized residual variances are approximately .815, .458, and .626. Std.all residual variances are .705, .509, and .673. For example, q04 has about .701 squared = .491 of its variance explained by the factor, leaving .509 unexplained. This squared-loading interpretation applies to the simple single-factor-per-item structure here.

```{r}
tab(lavInspect(fit3_marker, "cov.ov"), "Three-item implied covariance matrix")
# ML uses divisor N; base cov() uses N-1. Align them before comparison.
S_ml <- cov(dat[c("q03", "q04", "q05")]) * (nrow(dat)-1)/nrow(dat)
max(abs(S_ml - lavInspect(fit3_marker, "cov.ov")))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fitted(fit3_marker)$cov,
fitted(fit3_variance)$cov, tolerance = 1e-5)))
fit3_means <- cfa(m1a, data = dat, meanstructure = TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit3_means, c("npar", "df"))
```

The implied covariance matrix reproduces the corresponding ML sample matrix up to numerical tolerance. Both models have df=0, so chi-square=0 is a consequence of just-identification, not evidence that the three items form a valid scale. Adding means increases the free parameter count from six to nine, but df remains zero.

## Two-item identification example

A standalone two-item model has only three covariance moments. Without an extra restriction, marker scaling leaves four free parameters and the model is under-identified. The following teaching model imposes equal unstandardized loadings and fixes the factor variance to one, leaving one common loading and two residual variances. The equality is a substantive restriction, not a fact established by this saturated fit.

```{r}
fit2_equal <- cfa('f =~ a*q04 + a*q05', data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit2_equal, standardized = TRUE)
```

## Eight-item model and model-fit statistics

This model tests whether a single factor can account for the covariances across all eight items. There are 36 covariance moments, eight free loadings and eight residual variances under unit factor variance, giving df=20.

```{r}
m8 <- 'f =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q06 + q07 + q08'
fit8 <- cfa(m8, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
fit8_marker <- cfa(m8, data = dat)
summary(fit8, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
tab(parameters(fit8), "Eight-item loadings and residual variances")
tab(t(as.matrix(fitrow(fit8))), "Eight-item fit statistics")
```

The eight-item standardized loadings are approximately .586, -.233, -.570, .667, .574, .494, .650, and .486. Item 2 is weakest: its factor explains only about .233 squared, or 5.4%, of its variance. Item 4 has the largest loading magnitude. Signs are consistent with the observed relationships; significance of a loading does not make it strong or establish adequate overall fit.

The reproduced result is chi-square(20)=554.191, p<.001; CFI=.871; TLI=.819; RMSEA=.102, 90% CI [.095,.109], close-fit p<.001; and SRMR=.055. AIC is 53291.118 and BIC is 53384.751. The relatively small SRMR does not outweigh the weak CFI/TLI, high RMSEA, and rejection of exact fit. Taken together, the proposed single factor does not adequately represent all eight items.

| Statistic | Meaning and interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| Chi-square | Tests exact reproduction of population covariances. A small p-value rejects exact fit; large samples detect even small discrepancies. A large p-value does not prove the model. |
| CFI | Improvement over the independence baseline, adjusted using chi-square minus df. Values nearer 1 indicate better relative fit; .90/.95 are rough guides. |
| TLI | Baseline comparison that penalizes complexity using chi-square per df. Values nearer 1 are desirable; it is not universally bounded between 0 and 1. |
| RMSEA | Approximate discrepancy per df. About .05 or less suggests close fit and .05-.08 reasonable approximation; near .10 suggests poor fit. Interpret its CI and model context. |
| Close-fit p | Tests RMSEA <= .05. A small p rejects close fit; a large p does not prove it. |
| SRMR | Standardized observed-versus-implied residual summary; smaller is better, with .08 often used as a rough reference. |
| AIC/BIC | Relative information criteria: lower is preferred among suitable models fitted to the same observed variables and sample. They have no universal pass/fail cutoff. |

These are guides, not a voting system. The number of indicators, estimator, sample size, residual patterns, theory, and parameter plausibility must also be considered.

# Two-factor CFA

## Orthogonal and correlated models

The seminar removes q02 and assigns q01, q03, q04, q05, and q08 to SPSS Anxiety (f1), and q06/q07 to Attribution Bias (f2). The f2 label is illustrative because of the source's inconsistent item wording. An orthogonal model fixes f1 `~~` f2 to zero. Its two-item factor additionally requires equal loadings. A correlated model estimates the factor covariance and permits unequal f2 loadings.

```{r}
m_orth <- '
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
f2 =~ a*q06 + a*q07
f1 ~~ 0*f2
'
fit_orth <- cfa(m_orth, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
m_corr <- '
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
f2 =~ q06 + q07
'
fit_corr <- cfa(m_corr, data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit_orth, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
summary(fit_corr, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
tab(parameters(fit_orth), "Orthogonal model parameters")
tab(parameters(fit_corr), "Correlated model parameters")
```

The orthogonal model gives chi-square(15)=841.205, CFI=.786, TLI=.700, RMSEA=.146, and SRMR=.180. The q06/q07 unstandardized loadings are equal at approximately .797, but their standardized loadings differ (.710/.723) because their item variances differ. The zero covariance is imposed; it is not evidence that the constructs are unrelated.

The correlated model gives chi-square(13)=66.768, CFI=.986, TLI=.977, RMSEA=.040 with 90% CI [.031,.050], close-fit p about .952, and SRMR=.021. Its factor correlation is about .676. Standardized f1 loadings are .619, -.557, .694, .588, and .498; f2 loadings are .596 and .861. The squared loadings and residuals show that some items still have substantial unexplained variance despite good global approximate fit. Exact fit is rejected, but the overall approximate fit is much more favorable than the orthogonal model.

## Comparison on consistent indicators

The original eight-item and seven-item models use different observed variables, so their raw chi-squares, AIC, and BIC should not be used for a formal likelihood comparison. To isolate dimensionality, I also fit one factor to the same seven retained indicators. The orthogonal-versus-correlated seminar comparison changes both the covariance and the equality constraint; it does not isolate covariance alone.

```{r}
fit7 <- cfa('f =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q06 + q07 + q08',
data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
# Same equality constraint in both models isolates the covariance restriction.
fit_corr_equal <- cfa('
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
f2 =~ a*q06 + a*q07
', data = dat, std.lv = TRUE)
tab(rbind(One_factor_7 = fitrow(fit7), Orthogonal_7 = fitrow(fit_orth),
Correlated_equal_7 = fitrow(fit_corr_equal),
Correlated_7 = fitrow(fit_corr)), "Comparisons on seven indicators")
lavTestLRT(fit_orth, fit_corr_equal)
```

The equal-loading comparison tests only whether fixing the factor covariance to zero worsens fit. The general correlated model also relaxes equality of the two f2 loadings. A one-factor model corresponds to a limiting perfect-correlation condition within a two-factor formulation, so I do not treat an ordinary chi-square difference test of those models as automatically regular. Theory and the same-item fit pattern support keeping two correlated dimensions as the more defensible teaching conclusion.

# Second-order CFA

## Specification and interpretation

A higher-order factor represents a proposed common source of relationships among first-order factors. Here overall Anxiety (f3) predicts f1 and f2. First-order factors become endogenous and have disturbance variances in addition to item residual variances. With only two first-order indicators, the higher-order part needs additional constraints.

```{r}
m_higher <- '
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04 + q05 + q08
f2 =~ q06 + q07
f3 =~ 1*f1 + 1*f2
f3 ~~ f3
'
fit_higher <- cfa(m_higher, data = dat)
summary(fit_higher, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
tab(parameters(fit_higher), "Second-order parameters")
tab(rbind(Correlated = fitrow(fit_corr), Higher_order = fitrow(fit_higher)),
"Correlated and constrained higher-order fit")
stopifnot(max(abs(fitted(fit_corr)$cov - fitted(fit_higher)$cov)) < 1e-5)
```

Both higher-order loadings are fixed to one in the unstandardized metric. The estimated higher-order variance is about .232; standardized higher-order loadings are .939 for f1 and .720 for f2. The first-order disturbance variances are approximately .031 and .216, or .118 and .482 after standardization. Overall Anxiety accounts for about 88.2% of f1 variance and 51.8% of f2 variance under these constraints.

This specification reproduces the correlated model's implied covariance matrix and fit: chi-square(13)=66.768, CFI=.986, TLI=.977, RMSEA about .040, and SRMR=.021. Equal fit is not independent statistical evidence for a higher-order cause. With only two first-order factors and identifying constraints, the general factor is strongly assumption-dependent. I prefer the simpler correlated-factor description until theory, more first-order dimensions, and independent data justify a hierarchy.

# Practice questions and answers

## Canvas practice questions

1. **What is the difference between EFA and CFA?** EFA explores plausible latent structures; CFA tests a prespecified pattern of loadings and relationships. A model modified repeatedly from its own output needs validation in new data.

2. **What are the observed indicators and latent factors in SAQ-8?** q01-q08 are observed item responses. The one-factor model posits SPSS Anxiety. The retained seven-item model distinguishes SPSS Anxiety and the seminar's Attribution Bias factor; the higher-order example adds overall Anxiety.

3. **What do loadings represent?** They are regression coefficients from factors to indicators. A fully standardized loading such as .694 for q04 in the correlated model means a one-SD factor increase corresponds to a .694-SD expected item increase.

4. **What do residual variances represent?** They are variation left after the modeled factors. For q07 in the correlated model, the standardized residual is about .258, leaving approximately 74.2% explained.

5. **How many unique variances/covariances are available with three indicators?** There are 3(4)/2=6: three variances and three distinct covariances.

6. **Fixed versus free parameter?** A fixed loading of 1 defines a scale without being estimated; a free loading is estimated from data. An equality constraint permits estimation but requires two parameters to share a value.

7. **Why is negative df under-identified?** There are more independently unknown parameters than observed moments. The available moments cannot uniquely determine all unknown quantities.

8. **Why fix one loading and residual covariances?** Fixing the loading sets the factor's scale; fixing the three distinct residual covariances to zero imposes local-independence restrictions. Starting from ten quantities, 10-4=6 remain free, matching the six moments in the generic three-item case.

9. **Just-identified versus over-identified?** A just-identified model has zero df and no global covariance-fit test. An identified model with positive df imposes restrictions that can be tested. Positive df alone does not guarantee identification.

10. **How should chi-square, CFI, TLI, and RMSEA be interpreted?** Chi-square evaluates exact fit; CFI/TLI assess relative improvement over independence; RMSEA assesses approximate discrepancy per df. Interpret their pattern, confidence intervals, sample size, and theoretical plausibility rather than a single cutoff.

11. **Correlated versus uncorrelated factors?** The correlated model estimates covariance; the uncorrelated model fixes it to zero. In the seven-item example the estimated correlation is .676, and forcing orthogonality produces poor fit.

12. **What does a second-order factor represent?** It is a latent explanation of shared variation among first-order factors, which serve as its indicators. It accounts for part of their variance while allowing first-order disturbances.

13. **Which model is most appropriate?** Among the seminar examples, the seven-item correlated two-factor model offers strong approximate fit and an interpretable separation of dimensions. This is provisional: removing q02 changes content, and the identical higher-order fit does not identify a unique substantive explanation.

14. **What additional information is needed?** I would verify the original wording and reverse coding, sampling design, distribution and category frequencies, estimator suitability, residuals, reliability, convergent/discriminant evidence, and measurement invariance. I would seek independent validation and more indicators of f2; a two-item factor is fragile.

## Webpage quizzes and video polls

- **Why does marker scaling make the unrestricted three-item example just-identified?** Of ten unique candidate quantities, one loading and three residual covariances are fixed. Six remain free, so df=6-6=0.
- **What is df under variance scaling?** Fixing the factor variance and the same three residual covariances again leaves six unknowns and df=0.
- **Why do means not change df?** Three freely estimated intercepts add three parameters and three observed means: nine moments minus nine parameters remains zero.
- **Why is the eight-item one-factor df 20?** There are 36 moments minus 16 independent parameters: eight loadings and eight residual variances with unit factor variance.
- **Is the empirical residual covariance Sigma minus Sigma(theta)?** False as an empirical definition. It is S minus Sigma(theta-hat). The population expression equals zero under the exact-fit null.
- **Does larger chi-square mean larger residual covariance?** In the seminar's intended overall-discrepancy sense, generally yes at fixed N and model conditions. It does not imply that each residual grows, becomes positive, or can be compared without considering N and weighting.
- **For df=20 and chi-square/df <=2, what range is acceptable?** The seminar reports 20-40, but the literal upper-bound rule is chi-square<=40; nonnegative values below 20 are also compatible. A ratio of one is a reference expectation, not the only possible good-fitting value.
- **Does df=1 describe an over-identified model?** It supplies one over-identifying restriction, provided the parameters are identifiable.
- **Do three indicators supply six known covariance moments?** Yes, by symmetry and the p(p+1)/2 formula.
- **Do six unique parameters and no fixed parameters give df=0 with three indicators?** The arithmetic is 6-(6-0)=0. This alone does not prove that the particular parameterization is identifiable.
- **Is the goal to reject the covariance-fit null?** No. Rejection is evidence against exact fit; failure to reject does not prove the model true.
- **Does larger N increase the chance of rejection?** For a fixed nonzero population discrepancy, larger N increases power and usually the chi-square. It does not make every correctly specified model reject.
- **Does lavaan normally correlate exogenous CFA factors?** Yes. Specify a zero covariance explicitly when theory requires orthogonality.
- **Can both marker and variance scaling be used in two-factor CFA?** Yes, when each factor and the full model are identified; changing scale alone should not change fit.
- **Does setting a covariance to zero establish no association in the data?** No. It is a model assumption whose consequences can be evaluated through fit and parameter restrictions.

# Supplementary seminar exercises

## Exercise 1: all eight items and three reported metrics

The eight-item model above gives marker estimates, latent-standardized estimates, and fully standardized estimates. To make all three explicit in one output, the marker model is summarized below. The largest fully standardized loading is about .667 (q04), while q02 is only -.233. Weak measurement of q02 and evidence of multiple dimensions are plausible reasons for poor fit; automatic item deletion is not a substitute for theory.

```{r}
summary(fit8_marker, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
# The variance-scaled model should have equivalent fit.
stopifnot(abs(fitMeasures(fit8_marker,"chisq") - fitMeasures(fit8,"chisq")) < 1e-5)
```

## Exercise 2: four-plus-four allocation and item removal

This exercise uses a different item allocation from the main seven-item example. It assigns q01-q04 to f1 and q05-q08 to f2, then removes the lowest absolute standardized loading in each factor. The seminar identifies q02 and q08. The final comparison sets the covariance to zero in the reduced six-item model.

```{r}
ex_full <- cfa('
f1 =~ q01 + q02 + q03 + q04
f2 =~ q05 + q06 + q07 + q08
', data = dat)
ex_reduced <- cfa('
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04
f2 =~ q05 + q06 + q07
', data = dat)
ex_orth <- cfa('
f1 =~ q01 + q03 + q04
f2 =~ q05 + q06 + q07
f1 ~~ 0*f2
', data = dat)
tab(parameters(ex_full), "Exercise 2: initial item loadings")
tab(parameters(ex_reduced), "Exercise 2: retained item loadings")
tab(rbind(Full_8 = fitrow(ex_full), Reduced_6 = fitrow(ex_reduced),
Orthogonal_6 = fitrow(ex_orth)), "Exercise 2 fit results")
lavTestLRT(ex_orth, ex_reduced)
```

Removing q02/q08 improves CFI descriptively (the video reports about .917 for the reduced model), but TLI remains around .844, indicating the remaining structure is still imperfect. The eight-item and six-item models cannot be directly compared by a likelihood-ratio test or raw AIC/BIC because their observed variables differ. The six-item orthogonal versus correlated models use the same variables and are nested, so their likelihood-ratio comparison is appropriate under ML assumptions. Forcing zero covariance substantially worsens fit. Removing weak items is an exploratory action and needs content review and independent validation.

## Exercise 3: baseline, saturated model, and manual CFI

The independence baseline estimates each item's variance and fixes its covariances to zero. The saturated model estimates every unique variance and covariance, so its df is zero. To calculate CFI, the relevant quantities are the baseline and the user model chi-squares and degrees of freedom; the saturated model demonstrates the unconstrained benchmark.

```{r}
# Generate each unique variance/covariance statement once.
baseline_syntax <- paste(paste(items, "~~", items), collapse = "
")
saturated_syntax <- paste(vapply(seq_along(items), function(i) {
paste(items[i], "~~", paste(items[i:length(items)], collapse = " + "))
}, character(1)), collapse = "
")
cat(baseline_syntax, "

", saturated_syntax)
fit_base <- cfa(baseline_syntax, data = dat)
fit_sat <- cfa(saturated_syntax, data = dat)
tab(rbind(Baseline = fitMeasures(fit_base,c("chisq","df")),
Saturated = fitMeasures(fit_sat,c("chisq","df")),
User = fitMeasures(fit8,c("chisq","df"))),
"Exercise 3: covariance-model benchmarks")
u <- fitMeasures(fit8, c("chisq","df"))
b <- fitMeasures(fit_base,c("chisq","df"))
# This is the usual nonnegative correction form for CFI.
delta_u <- max(unname(u[1]-u[2]), 0)
delta_b <- max(unname(b[1]-b[2]), 0)
cfi_manual <- 1 - delta_u/max(delta_u,delta_b)
c(Manual_CFI = cfi_manual, lavaan_CFI = fitMeasures(fit8,"cfi"))
stopifnot(abs(cfi_manual-fitMeasures(fit8,"cfi")) < 1e-6)
```

The baseline result is chi-square=4164.572 with df=28; the user model is 554.191 with df=20. Thus CFI=1-(554.191-20)/(4164.572-28)=.871. The saturated model has chi-square approximately zero and df=0. This calculation uses the correct user-model values rather than the inconsistent values discussed during the video exercise.

# Summary of important lessons

CFA evaluates a proposed measurement structure through the relationship between observed and model-implied covariances. Establishing the factor scale and inspecting identification must precede interpreting results. Standardization changes units, while restrictions such as zero factor covariance change the model. A just-identified model can reproduce covariances without validating a scale. Global fit and individual measurement quality address different questions and both matter.

For SAQ-8, one factor fits poorly. The main seven-item correlated two-factor model gives good approximate fit, while orthogonality performs poorly. The constrained higher-order model has equivalent fit, so theory and better measurement are needed to justify a general factor. Any item deletion or data-driven change should be reported and checked with new data.

For my future PhD Orthodontics CEP survey work, the transferable lesson is to define constructs and indicator wording before analysis, verify coding, and validate measurement before relating constructs to marketing outcomes. This assignment analyzes UCLA's teaching data; it does not claim that the SAQ results describe orthodontic patients or that aggregate Google Ads metrics form reflective psychological scales.

## Reproduction and model diagnostics

Render m11-cfa-study-note.qmd with Quarto from the repository root. The repository contains the original UCLA teaching file; the analysis selects only its first eight items. The code is visible, output is calculated during rendering, and the HTML embeds its resources. The checks below confirm convergence and positive residual/latent variances for the main models; they do not establish substantive validity.

```{r}
models <- list(Three_item=fit3_marker, Eight_item=fit8,
Orthogonal=fit_orth, Correlated=fit_corr, Higher_order=fit_higher)
tab(data.frame(Model=names(models),
Converged=sapply(models,lavInspect,what="converged"),
Admissible=sapply(models,lavInspect,what="post.check")))
stopifnot(all(sapply(models,lavInspect,what="converged")),
all(sapply(models,lavInspect,what="post.check")))
sessionInfo()
```
